text.p: Advanta Corp, the Spring House, Pa.-based credit card issuer which earlier Monday said it expects a first quarter loss of about $0.44 per share, should show a profit in the second quarter of 1997, chief financial officer David Wesselink said in an interview.

"At the present time we expect to be back in the black in the second quarter and have increasing earnings in each subsequent quarter," he said. In announcing the surprise first quarter loss, Advanta said it expected a profit for the year 1997 of about $1.50 per share.
Alex "Pete" Hart, chief executive of Advanta, said in the interview that repricing of its credit products are a key to the turnaround.
"We believe demand for consumer credit will continue and the key is to price it appropriately," Hart said.
Asked if customers in good standing will now be paying more, Hart responded: "Some of those will be paying more and that's fairly consistent across the industry."
He said repricing would be selective and customers would pay "consistent with the risks they represent."
Hart said increased delinquencies and charge-offs of bad accounts have been "systemic" in the industry.

He said one reason for the trend was a sharp rise in personal bankruptcies in the U.S. The bankruptcies have been fueled by a change in the law in December 1994 and by a "changing attitude" among the public where bankruptcy has had less of a stigma than in years past.
The bankruptcy trend has been coupled with high household debt, he added.
Hart sidestepped a question about whether Advanta's problems could be tied to aggressive lending in 1996-1996, as suggested by analysts.

"It's always easy to look back," he said, adding that it must be remembered that credit is a cyclical business and, when consumers become pressed, they are less likely to pay on their unsecured credit.
In fact, he is encouraged about growth and returns in Advanta's other businesses, which include mortgage lending, leasing and insurance.

Advanta said in its news release that it hired BT Wolfensohn, a unit of Bankers Trust New York Co, to explore strategic alternatives. Asked what the firm would do specifically, vice chairman William Rosoff said only that "there are a lot of changes going on in the industry and a lot of potential opportunities."

Rosoff also declined to elaborate on why the company's board adopted a shareholder rights plan. Such plans are fairly common in a company's takeover defenses. The news release said the plan would "deter coerceive takeover tactics."
